question_type: Threshold count of investor categories holding a named security type (tax anticipation bills) across two Treasury Survey of Ownership dates

opus_path.decision: Read 'TABs' as Tax Anticipation Bills, a distinct sub-block of Treasury bills; 'total Treasury TABs' = sum of every TAB issue outstanding per investor category; 7 categories = insurance life+fire/casualty/marine combined, state/local general+pension combined, 'all other investors' excluded; 'recorded in March' = the March bulletin that prints the Jan-31 survey.
Used the March 1962 and March 1963 bulletins (surveys dated Jan 31); considered and rejected the end-of-March surveys printed in the May issues because the question names the January survey dates.

Section I Table 3 'Interest-Bearing Public Marketable Securities by Issues', 'Tax anticipation:' sub-block (two TAB issues in the 1962 survey, one in 1963); dropped the PDO Table 2 bill-offerings hit because it has no holder breakdown.

Ignored the OCR-garbled Table 3 headers and mapped columns by value identity: Table 2 'Treasury bills' row equals Table 3 'Total Treasury bills' row, which fixes the column order (USG accounts+F.R. Banks next-to-last, all other investors last) in both years.
opus_path.evidence: worklog.md:23 and 32; reviewer added the Table 1 'Special issues' row (held only by government accounts) as a label anchor, review.md check 3

opus_path.decision: Cross-footed each TAB row to its printed total and the bill sub-rows to 'Total Treasury bills' to confirm no TAB row was missing; treated '*' and '-' as zero.
opus_path.evidence: worklog.md:27, 35; calc.py row() and cross-foot print

opus_path.decision: calc.py reads the cited rows straight from the corpus, sums per category across TAB issues, counts categories above the threshold per year, adds the two counts.
Threshold sensitivity (only one value near the threshold, clearly below it), aggregation sensitivity (per-issue vs summed gives the same count), alternative-reading count computed and rejected.

opus_key_moves: Took the acronym literally (TAB = tax anticipation bill) and used the 'Tax anticipation:' sub-block, summing all TAB issues per category instead of using the all-bills total row.

Established column order by matching identical rows across Table 2 and Table 3 (and, in review, the government-only 'Special issues' row) instead of trusting the shifted OCR header, which in the 1963 table carries a spurious extra column label.
Cross-footed every TAB row and the bill block to printed totals before counting.

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Right source, right table, right TAB rows and right aggregation. But it read the 1963 TAB row against the 1963 Table 3 OCR header, which has a spurious extra 'State and local governments' column label before 'U.S. Government investment accounts and Federal Reserve Banks'. It assigned the next-to-last value to a state/local aggregate and the last value (which is actually 'Held by all other investors', well above the threshold) to USG accounts+F.R. Banks, treating the trailing 'nan' cell as 'all other'. That added one spurious category above the threshold in 1963; its 1962 count was right.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Mapped the Table 3 columns by matching the Table 3 'Total Treasury bills' row to the Table 2 'Treasury bills' row (treasury_bulletin_1963_03.txt:3717 vs :3769). This shows 1963 uses the same 10-value order as 1962 (USG+FR next-to-last, all other last). The reviewer confirmed it with the Table 1 'Special issues' row.
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: It saw the inconsistency. At [17] it noted that its supposed state/local 'aggregate' was larger than general+pension ('So state/local aggregate not sum of general/pension'). At [20] it asked 'Why 1963 has aggregate but 1962 not?'. It then treated the fact that the ten 1963 values cross-foot to the total as confirmation of its labeling, but cross-footing works for any labeling. It never used a label-independent anchor. In the 1962 table it resolved the same question correctly by arithmetic, but it did not carry that column order over to 1963.
first_divergence.consequence: USG+FR was counted as above $500M in 1963, so the final sum is one category too high (>25% relative error).

secondary_errors.note: Its robustness check varied only the TAB aggregation (March-maturity row only vs all TAB issues) and declared the count 'robust'. It never varied the column mapping, which was the actual open uncertainty.

remedies.intervention: Header/data column reconciliation on flattened tables. When a header has more labels than non-empty value columns (the 1963 Table 3 header has one more label than there are values, plus a trailing all-nan column), flag the header as shifted and require the column mapping to be proven by a label-independent anchor: a row known to sit in exactly one column (the government-only 'Special issues' row) or an identical total row in a sibling table.
remedies.why: GLM detected the 10-vs-11 mismatch at [20] but had no procedure to resolve it. The anchor step is exactly what Opus (worklog.md:23, 32) and its reviewer (review.md check 3) did.

remedies.intervention: Table extractor that returns a clean grid: drops all-nan trailing columns, reconciles header labels to value columns by count, and aligns columns across the tables of one section (TSO Tables 1-3) by matching identical rows.
remedies.why: The garble is systematic. The 1962 and 1963 headers are shifted in different ways, and the actor read labels at face value in both. A pre-aligned grid would remove the decision entirely.

remedies.intervention: Pre-commit sensitivity step that must list every uncertain choice (including column mapping) and recompute under each alternative; if the answer changes, block commit until the choice is resolved with evidence.
remedies.why: At [22] the actor ran a robustness check but only over interpretation. A checklist that names 'column mapping' would have shown the 1963 count flips.

first_divergence.what_glm_did: Treated 'total Treasury TABs' as a typo for the 'Total Treasury bills' row (all bills) of TSO Table 3, and counted categories above $500M on that row in each survey. On the all-bills row most categories exceed the threshold, so the count comes out far too high.
first_divergence.what_opus_did: Read TABs as tax anticipation bills and used the 'Tax anticipation:' sub-block, summing TAB issues per category.
first_divergence.why_glm_went_that_way: At [1], before seeing any table, it guessed 'TABs maybe typo bills?'. At [14] it explicitly stated the right reading ('Tax anticipation bills (TABs) are a type of Treasury bill'). It then grepped the literal string 'TABs' ([15], empty) and took the empty result to mean the term is not in the corpus. It chose the 'Total Treasury bills' row at [18]-[20] because the row name shares the words 'Total Treasury' with the question. Its adapter's TSO lessons describe the TSO-3 bill block as maturity rows plus a 'Total Treasury Bills' row (the 1977 layout) and never mention a tax-anticipation block, which may have made that row feel like the canonical target.
first_divergence.consequence: Counted categories on the wrong row; the answer is several times the reference (>25%).

adapter_context.notes: The cadence rule (end-of-January survey printed in the March bulletin) is correct and was followed from [1]. The layout rule describes the 1977 bill block ('12 maturity rows + Total Treasury Bills') and says nothing about the early-1960s 'Tax anticipation:' sub-block. That emphasis on the 'Total Treasury Bills' row plausibly reinforced the typo reading. No lesson defines TABs. After this episode the learner added a correct postmortem lesson (seen in later AGENTS.md copies, e.g. the 072 copy at :735-753) with 'grep for Tax anticipation, never for TABs'.

remedies.intervention: Term-grounding step before table selection: for each domain noun or acronym in the question, list candidate expansions and grep each one in the located table; a 'the question contains a typo' reading is allowed only if no expansion matches. Here the expansion 'tax anticipation' matches a sub-block header in the very table in hand.
remedies.why: The actor produced the correct expansion itself at [14] and had the matching rows on screen at [11]/[13]/[17]. What it lacked was a rule to prefer a literal reading grounded in the corpus over a typo hypothesis. An empty grep for the literal acronym at [15] tipped it the wrong way.

remedies.intervention: Lesson: 'TABs = tax anticipation bills. In 1950s-60s TSO Table 3 they form a separate Tax anticipation: block under Treasury bills. Sum the block's issues per holder. Never grep the acronym itself.'
remedies.why: This arm followed its TSO cadence lesson exactly, so a table-specific lesson in the same form would likely be followed. The learner wrote this lesson after the fact.

remedies.intervention: Lexical check between the question and the cited row: if the key noun in the question (TABs) does not appear in the chosen row or block label (bills), return a warning that asks for a justification or a re-search.

right_arms_note: cards: at the interpretation point it took TABs literally and used the 'Tax anticipation:' block, which was principled. At the 1963 column-mapping point it read values in the 1962 positional order and ignored the extra header label. The result was correct, but it ran no explicit check, so this part was partly luck: it faced the same header trap that caught the none arm.
text_vs_mechanism: These are two different failures. The prompt arm's typo reading could plausibly be fixed by a TAB-definition lesson, but it had already produced the right expansion itself and rejected it, so a term-grounding CONTROL is more reliable. The none arm's column misread needs a mechanism (label-anchor CHECK or clean-grid TOOL). The prompt arm's own convention 'match columns by header, never by position' (AGENTS.md:51-57) points the wrong way when OCR headers are shifted, as they are here.
notes: The postmortem lesson the prompt learner wrote afterwards says to confirm column order 'by summing the holder columns into the printed total'. The none arm did exactly that and still mislabeled, because cross-footing cannot tell which column is USG+FR and which is 'all other'. Only a label anchor can (the government-only 'Special issues' row, or the identity of the Table 2 and Table 3 total rows). A harness check for shifted headers should use anchors, not sums. All three arms opened the right March bulletins, so source selection was not the problem.
